problems.title: Single Number
problems.statement: Every number in the array appears exactly twice except one. Find that single number. You must solve it in O(n) time and O(1) space.
problems.understanding: XOR has two golden properties: x ^ x = 0 (pairs cancel) and x ^ 0 = x (identity). XOR-ing all elements causes every duplicate pair to vanish, leaving only the unique number.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Use a hash set: add unseen numbers, remove them when seen a second time. Whatever remains is the answer.

problems.intuition: XOR all elements together. Paired numbers cancel to 0. The single unpaired number XOR'd with 0 returns itself.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Pairs + one unique → XOR all elements (x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x)

problems.title: Number of 1 Bits
problems.statement: Given an unsigned integer, return the number of set bits (1s) in its binary representation (Hamming weight).
problems.understanding: n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit. Repeating this until n == 0 tells us exactly how many 1-bits exist — one iteration per set bit, not per total bit.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Check all 32 bits one by one using n & 1 and right-shift.

problems.intuition: n - 1 flips the lowest set bit and all bits below it. So n & (n-1) removes exactly the lowest 1-bit. Each iteration costs one set bit — loop runs exactly k times where k is the Hamming weight.

optimal.title: Optimized Code (Python 3)
complexity: Time: O(k) — k = number of set bits

problems.takeaway: Pattern — n & (n-1) removes the lowest set bit — loop runs once per 1-bit

problems.title: Counting Bits
problems.statement: Given n, return an array of length n+1 where result[i] is the number of 1-bits in i.
problems.understanding: Right-shifting a number by 1 removes its last bit: num >> 1 has the same 1-bits as num minus the contribution of its last bit. So bits[num] = bits[num >> 1] + (num & 1) — build on already-computed results.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: For each number 0..n, count its 1-bits independently using n & (n-1).

problems.intuition: DP recurrence: bits[num] = bits[num >> 1] + (num & 1). Removing the last bit gives a smaller number whose bit count is already known.

problems.title: Reverse Bits
problems.statement: Reverse the bits of a given 32-bit unsigned integer and return the result.
problems.understanding: Extract the rightmost bit of n using n & 1, shift it into the leftmost available position of result using result <<= 1 then result |= n & 1, then right-shift n. Repeat 32 times.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Build a binary string of n, reverse it, then reconstruct the integer.

problems.intuition: Per-iteration: shift result left to make room, OR in the lowest bit of n, then right-shift n. After 32 iterations the bits are fully reversed.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Shift + extract each bit: result <<= 1 → result |= (n & 1) → n >>= 1

problems.title: Missing Number
problems.statement: Given an array containing n distinct numbers from [0, n], return the one missing number.
problems.understanding: XOR the complete range 0..n with every element of the array. Present numbers cancel in pairs; only the missing number has no partner to cancel with.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Put all numbers in a set; scan 0..n for the missing one.

problems.intuition: Start with answer = n. For each index i, XOR in both i and nums[i]. Every index 0..n-1 is covered, and each present number cancels. The missing number survives.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Missing value in known range → XOR complete range with array (also solvable as sum(0..n) - sum(nums))

problems.title: Sum of Two Integers
problems.statement: Calculate a + b without using the operators + or -.
problems.understanding: a ^ b computes the sum bit-by-bit ignoring carries. (a & b) << 1 produces the carry bits shifted into position. Repeat, treating the carry as the new addend, until there is no carry left.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: In Python, just return a + b — but this violates the constraint.

problems.intuition: Binary addition: XOR gives the digit sum without carry; AND gives where carries occur, shifted left one position. Mask to 32 bits to simulate fixed-width arithmetic. Handle sign extension at the end for negative results.
problems.approach:
1. Set MASK = 0xFFFFFFFF (32 bits), MAX_INT = 0x7FFFFFFF.
  2. While b != 0: compute carry = (a & b) << 1.
  3. a = (a ^ b) & MASK, b = carry & MASK.
  4. If a <= MAX_INT return a, else return ~(a ^ MASK) (sign-extend negative).
problems.takeaway: Pattern — XOR = addition without carry; (a & b) << 1 = carry; repeat until carry is 0

problems.title: Reverse Integer
problems.statement: Given a signed 32-bit integer x, return x with its digits reversed. If the reversed value overflows the 32-bit signed range [-2³¹, 2³¹-1], return 0.
problems.understanding: Extract digits right-to-left using x % 10 and rebuild the reversed number using result * 10 + digit. Handle sign separately. Check overflow against 32-bit bounds before returning.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Convert to string, reverse, convert back to int, then check overflow.

problems.intuition: Digit extraction: x % 10 gives the last digit; x //= 10 removes it. Accumulate into result = result * 10 + digit. Multiply sign back in at the end and validate the 32-bit range.
problems.approach:
1. Store sign = -1 if x < 0 else 1, then x = abs(x).
  2. Initialize result = 0.
  3. While x > 0: digit = x % 10, result = result * 10 + digit, x //= 10.
  4. result *= sign.
  5. If result is outside [-2³¹, 2³¹-1]: return 0; else return result.
problems.takeaway: Pattern — Digit extraction right-to-left: digit = x % 10, remove with x //= 10, rebuild with result * 10 + digit
